title: On Certifying Source Sampling Hardness in Quantum Generative Modeling
authors: Chen-Yu Liu, Leonardo Placidi, Enrico Rinaldi
abstract: Quantum generative models are often motivated by circuit families whose output distributions are believed to be classically hard to sample from. When such models are trained on ordinary classical datasets, however, this hardness does not automatically transfer to the unknown data-generating distribution. We show that transferring sampling hardness via total-variation closeness from a quantum model to an unknown source requires certifying a global relation between the two distributions, thereby reducing the problem to distribution certification. Combining this reduction with existing certification lower bounds yields an exponential sample requirement for the high-entropy distributions relevant to many sampling-hardness proposals. Consequently, polynomially many samples cannot, in general, justify attributing sampling hardness to an unknown data-generating distribution. Moreover, even classically trivial distributions, such as the uniform distribution and product distributions, require exponentially many samples to certify in the absence of structural assumptions. Our results clarify the role of sampling hardness in quantum generative modeling and distinguish generator-level hardness from source-level hardness when learning from ordinary datasets.
summary: This work analyzes the theoretical link between quantum generative models and the hardness of sampling from unknown data sources. It proves that transferring sampling hardness requires solving a difficult distribution certification problem, which demands exponentially many samples. Consequently, practitioners cannot generally assume that polynomial sampling efforts are enough to justify claiming source-level sampling hardness.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether the sampling hardness property of a quantum generative model can be reliably transferred to an unknown, real-world data-generating distribution when trained on finite classical samples.
main_result: Transferring sampling hardness requires certifying a global relationship between the two distributions, which necessitates an exponentially large number of samples for high-entropy distributions, meaning polynomial samples are generally insufficient.
method: The authors reduce the hardness transfer problem to a distribution certification problem, utilizing existing lower bounds from identity testing and total-variation distance analysis.
model_or_system: The focus is on Quantum Generative Models (QGMs) based on quantum circuit families, comparing the inherent hardness of the generator itself (generator-level hardness) versus the hardness of the unknown source distribution (source-level hardness).
key_observables: Total-Variation Distance ($d_{TV}$), Sample Requirement ($m$), Min-Entropy ($h$), and the $\ell_1$-distance threshold ($ho$).
important_parameters: The required sample complexity is shown to scale exponentially with the entropy of the distribution, and the analysis distinguishes between the complexity of the known-target certification problem and statistical fitting.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the most favorable certification setting (known target distribution, unlimited computational power) and relies on established lower bounds for identity testing.
paper_structure: The paper first distinguishes between generator-level and source-level hardness, then establishes that transferring hardness requires solving a distribution certification problem, which is then bounded by known lower bounds derived from identity testing.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous theoretical constraint on the claims made in quantum machine learning, showing that simply training a quantum model does not guarantee that the unknown data source possesses the desirable computational hardness property.
